day's command probes are exec'd directly, not through a shell: the command is split on whitespace and run as argv, so $(...), globs and redirections never expand. A probe using them fails with a usage error rather than a useful answer. Keep probes shell-metacharacter-free.

kan is append-only, so re-issuing a schema claim does not replace the old one — every version stays live and day reads one of them. Superseding a schema means retracting the previous claim by CID. Three schema/witness versions were live at once here, and assessments ran against the oldest.

check-fork had a defect that an exit-code-only negative test could not catch: divergence_reason returned non-zero when no path matched, so set -e killed the script at the first undeclared drift. It exited 1 without printing the DRIFT line and without checking the remaining files. Assert on the output of a negative test, not just its status.

Verify an exit code directly, never through a pipe. 'cmd | tail -3; echo $?' reports tail's status, and this session made that mistake three times - once concluding a Thermite gate 'exits 0' on a missing tomllib when it exits 3, which went into a PR description and needed a public correction. Use 'cmd > /tmp/out 2>&1; echo $?' or check PIPESTATUS. The same class of error appeared in a probe where a test failed on EnsIsTrivial rather than the precondition being tested, so the verdict was real and about the wrong thing.

A cheap reversible check makes wrong work cost nothing. The migration tool rewrites in both directions so 'to_v2(to_v3(x)) == x' can be run over the whole corpus in one command, and that turned two wrong implementations into two reverts instead of two shipped defects - inline-contract handling dropped it from 384/384 to 329/384 twice and was backed out both times. Two complements worth remembering: the round-trip is silent about what a tool FAILS to touch, so under-migration was found by the test suite rather than the proof; and a proof that a rewrite loses no information says nothing about whether the result means the same to the prover, which only re-certifying establishes.

Keys are per-device and roles are separate: each machine carries its own authentication key and its own signing key, all registered, so no private key is ever copied between hosts and a signature verifies whichever machine made it. Verified end to end rather than assumed - the key registered on GitHub as a signing key was initially the old auth key, which would have produced commits that verify locally and read Unverified upstream, and it was caught by comparing key material rather than titles.

A round-trip proves information preservation and is silent about coverage, because text a tool never touches is restored perfectly. thermite-migrate.py reported 382/382 files restoring byte for byte while failing to touch every one-line contract AND 17 @bv-tagged clauses across 10 files - ens@bv64, inv@bv8, ens@bv32(nowrap) - which the clause pattern did not match. A migrated corpus would have carried ens@bv64 into a front end with no ens keyword, and no round-trip run could have reported it. The general shape: a reversibility check scores what a tool DID, never what it SKIPPED, so it must be paired with a completeness check that asks whether any input construct survived the transformation unchanged. Here that check is one line - after migration, assert zero v2 clause tokens remain - and it is what found both gaps.
